children: The discussion over rogue artificial intelligence isn't going away anytime soon-in part because AI keeps going rogue.

An OpenAI agent breached the Australian Medicare statistics database in June, gaining access to nonpublic files, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed. The Australian government doesn't believe the agent accessed any personal information at this time.

Separately, OpenAI agents attempted to hack into three targets between May and June, according to a report from Transluce, a nonprofit AI researcher. The targets were another Australian government health portal, the University of New Mexico digital library, and Data USA, a nongovernment site providing access to public U.S. government data.
"Notably, the tasks the agents were trying to solve were not cyber-related," the Transluce researchers wrote. "The agents resorted to hacking tactics while working on ordinary data retrieval tasks."

An OpenAI spokesperson said much of the activity in Transluce's report overlaps with cases the company is investigating in its broader review of agents taking actions not aligned with human instructions.

The news comes ahead of President Donald Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday. Trump has pushed back on calls to implement international guardrails on the pace of AI development.

"Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also," Trump wrote in a social media post Thursday morning. "Our guardrail is the DOJ!"

Already, the worldwide discussion over AI safety-triggered in part by OpenAI agents breaching the Hugging Face developer platform over the summer-has taken center stage at the United Nations General Assembly.

In a press conference at UNGA, Albanese said he spoke with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to express "extreme concern" about the Medicare hack and his disappointment with how OpenAI disclosed it. The AI developer first sent an email to an Australian government public inbox on Sept. 10., Albanese added.
Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei both warned the U.N. Security Council on Wednesday about the need to control AI development. Executives at Microsoft and SpaceX have echoed their concerns.
